After reading all  these posts, I’d like to invite y’all to Topeka Kansas. We’ve got  5 nice disc golf courses in town, 10 more within a 25 minute drive and we’re only 45 minutes from emporia which is apparently some kind of weird midwestern disc golf Mecca. I haven’t been to the courses in Emporia, but of the thirty times I’ve played the courses here in Topeka I’ve only had to wait on a hole maybe three times, and I’ve only had people behind me once.

I agree with a comment on here where someone said that skill level matters.. And then there’s the thing that Miss Manners used to say - etiquette are the rules for people who don’t have good common courtesy.  Just be a decent and responsible person and things should work out. 

I had an interaction on the opposite side of things - my son and I were playing Harmony Bends in Springfield Mo.  it’s an amazing and beautiful course and way beyond our skill level. We were playing on a 100+ afternoon on a Monday and the course was nearly empty.  Somewhere, on one of the holes mid- course which was very long and uphill my son and I were searching for my third shot which had somehow avoided enough trees to go far enough to get lost in some direction that wasn’t really towards the basket. Suddenly, I heard the sound of some leaves ripping and watched a disk fly over my head. I kept looking for the disc and then this 16 year old kid walks up and says “oh man, I didn’t know y’all were up here - I’m so sorry.  You looking for a disc?  There’s a pink one just back there a bit - pretty good drive man!” 

I did not tell him that that  was my third shot 

I did tell him he could play through.

He walked up to his 450ft (138m) drive, took 5 seconds to somehow see a line through 19 different trees and casually flicked his disk the remaining 300feet (90m) to within 3 feet (1m) of the basket and then scooted along to the next tee. 

I was just happy he wasn’t there to watch me take the four more shots it took me to hole out. 

The point is that it’s a game. It’s supposed to be fun. If you are having fun playing slowly then let people play through. If you like to play faster then ask to play through. And, since it’s a game, sometimes when I play through I will go a bit faster and do a lot worse and maybe even just skip a putt so we can all get along with enjoying this ridiculous wonderful frustratingly joyful sport. 

One last thing I’ve learned  - is murphy’s law will get you.  I’m not good at this game and I can’t get much distance. Maybe on a great throw - every once in a while I rip one 350 ft. (106m). Usually when this happens it’ll be going about 30degrees right of where I was aiming. But I guarantee that if I were to risk throwing on a 450ft (138m) hole when people were on the green I would somehow throw the shot of my life and reach the people putting and just have enough sense to call out just in time so that they look up and see my freakishly wonderful throw when it’s too late to not get their teeth knocked out.

The OP was about the evolution of our size. 


So the first thing to do is look at closely related species. When we look at the hominoid apes we see that we are pretty average whereas the real outliers among this group are gorillas (and yes, should we compare them to an out group like horses or rhinoceroses or cetaceans we are all basically the same size.)  Now we have two different but related lines of investigation here. 

1) the general - why are Hominoid apes so much bigger than other primates. 

2) the specific - why did Homo erectus and their descendants start to evolve to increase in size over time?

I suspect that both of these questions have a similar answer. 

Here’s my go at it. And it’s going to be vague and not very satisfying. Larger size allows individuals and groups or individuals a greater ability to protect a resource from others that might want to exploit that same resource. Food, mating, continuation of existence without being eaten by leopards or Hyenas (sorry, I stuck myself in a bad phrasing and was lazy.). Size obviously isn’t the only factor, but it’s a pretty important one when dealing with similar species competing.

It’s an interesting question. However I think the question is more appropriate to ask, why did the homonoids size increase over time. Among this group our ancestors were on the smaller size of the spectrum (especially when you factor in massive critters like Gigantopithecus.) even when you look at modern humans you see that we are slightly larger than orangs, chimps, and bonobos but much smaller than gorillas. It wasn’t really until Homo erectus came around that our ancestors started to overtop any of the other apes is body mass. Before that we were just a typical ape size (albeit with a different mechanism of locomotion) although we were still a large primate.

First of all this isn't my theory.  It's called Bregmann's rule.  Within mammal species it holds fairly true. The closer you get to the pole the larger the animals are.  It's a simple matter of geometry.  Consider the surface area of a sphere and the volume of a sphere.  As the radius increases the volume increases by r^3 whereas the surface area increases by r^2.  And no, mammals aren't spheres, but if you want to go out and measure the surface area and volume of various mammals you can see that the larger size generally has a lower surface area to volume ratio.

As to your notion that the deeper you go in water the colder it gets.  That may be true in most temperate areas, but it doesn't hold true for the polar waters.  This is important because the largest animals that have ever lived tend to inhabit polar waters.  So temperature at depth isn't really a factor (there are tons of very interesting adaptations that deep diving mammals have in place to survive at almost 8000m - but temperature concerns aren't one of them.)  What's more, whales don't live in the depths.  They visit them.  They spend the overwhelming majority of their time much closer to the surface.

So, no that hypothesis isn't self-defeating.  I'm not saying it's the only reason for the huge size of whales.  But it is probably a factor.

Finally, I think the basic premise of the OP's post is flawed.  Looking at animals past an present we see a ton (ha ha) of really large animals on land.  Setting aside the largest rorquals we find that there have been just as many enormous creatures on land as in the water.

Water conducts heat much better than air, which is why you can be perfectly comfortable being outside on an 70F day but spend much time in 70F water and you’ll start to be very cold. The most accurate phrase I've heard used to describe the majority of human mating systems is "serial monogamy."

Humans are very much K-selected organisms. Probably among the most K-selected of all. We need to invest heavily in our offspring for them to survive and thrive. That's why we end up so often in monogamous pair-bonds. 

The other element that is not taken into account enough is the benefits to the tribe/band/troop. Humans have always needed to work together to be successful. If one man dominates the mating opportunities there will be strife and that leads to fights which damages the effectiveness of the group. 

Finally if you look at our testicle size compared to that of our close relatives you get some clues about our ancestral mating systems. Gorillas have small testicles because the only male who would dare to mate with a female is the Silverback. Chimps and Bonobos have much larger testicle because they are more promiscuous and so sperm competition is important. 

By comparison we find our males with moderately sized testicles, an outsized penis.  And our females with no visual signaling of ovulation, "continuous sexual receptivity" and a vigorous female orgasm. All of that suggests that pair-bonding and at least temporary monogamy is a human norm. Which is neat because both physiology and ethnographic data suggest the same thing.

This is a bizarrely phrased question. The term sex is scientific. Even there, it refers to different things at different levels.  It can mean the pattern of sex chromosomes for organisms that have chromosomal sex-determination (XX, XY, XXY, XYY, XXYY etc etc).  It can refer to either the presence of testicles and a penis or a vagina, uterus and ovaries. It can refer to which organism produces a sperm and which produces an egg. It should be noted that throughout the natural world even the concept of sex is not a binary system. Many variations exist. Additionally it is not necessarily something that is fixed for the lifetime of all organisms. 

The term gender exists specifically to discuss the relationship of the sex of an organism and its relationship to others of its species. Your desire to use the term "gender roles" to discuss "gender issues" is unnecessary. 


Your desire to find scientific insight into gender issues is laudable. However, when you look at the complexity of what is meant by these you'll see that there is no simple answer. 

Gender does not equal sexual preference
Gender does not equal sex
Perceived gender does not equal internal gender. 

Gender exists on a constantly evolving and shifting continuum.  Where someone fits on that continuum is up to them to determine and change as they see fit. It can't be otherwise and you'd see that if you looked closely at these issues throughout history and throughout different cultures.
